extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (petitioners and patent owners) who litigate AIA proceedings before the PTAB
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and legal guidance for preserving and litigating due process and APA rights in AIA inter partes review (IPR) proceedings after the Supreme Court’s SAS Institute v. Iancu decision. Focuses on what parties and the Board must do at institution and in briefing to avoid midstream theory changes and preserve appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA notice requirement (5 U.S.C. § 554(b)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the APA, 'Persons entitled to notice of an agency hearing shall be timely informed of . . . the matters of fact and law asserted.' This protection has been applied to both patent owners and petitioners in PTAB proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that the Board must timely inform parties of the matters of fact and law it asserts; Federal Circuit cases (e.g., SAS I) apply §554(b)(3) to petitioners as well as patent owners because petitioners are not disinterested and face estoppel consequences. Use institution decision and briefing to ensure parties receive this notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process essentials: notice and opportunity to be heard
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The indispensable ingredients of due process are notice and an opportunity to be heard by a disinterested decision-maker.' The APA requires the PTAB to provide timely information of asserted matters and an opportunity to submit facts and argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating procedural fairness, courts focus on whether parties were given adequate notice of case-dispositive issues and a meaningful chance to respond; lack of either can support setting aside agency action under §706.

rubrics_metrics.name: No change of theories 'in midstream' without notice and opportunity
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency may not 'change theories in midstream without giving respondents reasonable notice of the change and the opportunity to present argument under the new theory.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the PTAB bases its final decision on a new theory that was not presented earlier, the Federal Circuit has found APA/due process violations (examples: Dell, In re NuVasive). Conversely, where the basis was raised in petition/institution/oral argument and parties had a chance to respond, no violation is found (examples: BASF, Anacor). The 'new theory' must have served as the basis for the decision to trigger protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where and when a case-dispositive issue is first raised controls availability of a meaningful opportunity to be heard
rubrics_metrics.description: For due process analysis courts examine where and when a determinative issue was first raised and whether that provided sufficient notice and opportunity to meaningfully respond in briefing or oral argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a determinative issue is first raised in the final written decision or late (e.g., at oral argument without opportunity for sur-reply), that supports finding a due process violation; if it was introduced earlier (petition, institution decision, oral argument where parties debated), courts often find parties had a meaningful opportunity to be heard.

rubrics_metrics.name: The petition defines the scope of review; petitioners must raise all arguments in the petition
rubrics_metrics.description: The petition, not the Board, defines the scope of instituted review; petitioners must raise all potential arguments and claim construction positions in the petition or risk forfeiture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites SAS II and 35 U.S.C. §312(a)(3): failure to include arguments/claim constructions in the petition can forfeit the right to rely on them later (e.g., in reply). Practitioners should ensure petitions comprehensively present arguments they may later need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel (35 U.S.C. § 315(e)) presumes prior opportunity to be heard; petitioners entitled to APA protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Inter partes review estoppel prevents successive challenges, but its application presumes a party previously had an opportunity to challenge the patent; to avoid wrongful estoppel, petitioners are afforded APA protections and the right to appeal alleged violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a petitioner lacked a meaningful opportunity to be heard before estoppel attaches, estoppel may be wrongfully applied; courts have questioned standing in some circumstances (Consumer Watchdog, Phigenix) — practitioners should watch standing and preservation of hearing opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency required in claim construction between institution and final written decision
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTAB may not inconsistently construe claim terms between its institution decision and its final written decision without giving the parties an opportunity to be heard, because that would be a change of theories midstream.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent owners should consider raising claim construction positions in preliminary responses since winning a preliminary construction can be significant; if the Board alters a construction without notice, that can be grounds for APA reversal (SAS I, WesternGeco). When a party puts a construction at issue, the Board may alter it but must give opportunity to respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB has discretion on how much analysis to include in institution decisions; analysis of one representative claim is permissible but can be risky
rubrics_metrics.description: Statute and PTAB practice allow the Board discretion in institution decisions (35 U.S.C. §318(a)); the Board may analyze only one representative claim and need not evaluate every claim individually after SAS II.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although Alcatel‑Lucent shows analysis of a representative claim can suffice, the Federal Circuit has implied institution guidance is necessary to avoid due process violations. Limiting analysis may limit what the Board can later rely upon in a final written decision; panels are encouraged to continue providing full analysis where appropriate to guide parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: SAS II's practical effect: lowered incentive for fulsome institution analysis and increased burden on patent owners
rubrics_metrics.description: SAS II abolished partial institution, so if one claim shows reasonable likelihood of success the entire petition may be instituted, which can disincentivize the Board from analyzing all claims/grounds in depth at institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of this, patent owners face higher hurdles to avoid institution and should be more likely to file preliminary responses to develop counterarguments and claim constructions early to preserve bases for patentability at final decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution decisions can (and should) shape and frame subsequent briefing; lack of guidance risks APA appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: An institution decision can give notice of, frame, and focus the parties' subsequent briefing on case-dispositive issues; without such guidance parties may not be on notice of the issues the Board will treat as dispositive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EmeraChem demonstrates that when the Board's institution decision does not make clear reliance on a particular reference but the final decision does, the patent owner lacks notice and due process is violated. Parties should read institution orders carefully and respond to issues the Board signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use procedural safeguards to preserve ability to appeal (sur-reply, motion to observe evidence, rehearing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties must use built-in PTAB procedures — e.g., leave to file motion for observation of evidence, leave to file a sur-reply to address new evidence/argument, or rehearing of a final written decision — to preserve their right to appeal an alleged due process violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite 37 C.F.R. §§42.51(b)(2)(i), 42.20(b), 42.71(d) and the Patent Trial Practice Guide. The Federal Circuit has refused to find a due process violation where a party did not use available procedural safeguards (Belden, Securus). Failure to timely use these options can result in waiver or forfeiture of an APA appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: To succeed on an APA appeal, must show denial of a meaningful opportunity to be heard on a case-dispositive issue
rubrics_metrics.description: An appeal under the APA requires showing that the party was denied a meaningful opportunity to be heard on a case-dispositive issue, i.e., that the party lacked sufficient notice and chance to respond to the basis of the decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal Circuit holdings (Dell, In re NuVasive) emphasize that courts will reverse only where the new theory materially deprived the party of opportunity to respond; parties must preserve issues and use procedural remedies promptly to satisfy appellate standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish new factual grounds used as 'motivation' from new theories used as invalidating basis
rubrics_metrics.description: When the PTAB uses factual aspects of a reference merely to describe the state of the art or to motivate a combination, courts have found no due process violation; but using a reference as an unanticipated primary invalidating basis without notice can violate the APA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novartis and Genzyme show that reliance on references for motivation (when parties were aware of the references) is less likely to be reversible, while reliance on a reference as the primary invalidating ground when it was not clear from the institution decision can support reversal. Parties should address all cited references and their possible roles in both petition and preliminary response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency requirement: the Board should avoid a 'black box' decisionmaking process
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board cannot create a 'black box' process; institution decisions and panel practice should provide sufficient analysis so parties understand case-dispositive issues and can meaningfully respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shaw Industries (Reyna, J., concurring) and other Federal Circuit guidance urge panels to provide transparent reasoning. Post‑SAS practice shows many panels continue to analyze all claims and grounds to guide parties; where possible, panels should provide fuller analysis to reduce risk of APA reversal.
